summary:
Team StarX_TN developed StarX Health, an offline-first interactive prototype for astronaut health monitoring and self-management. It brings heart and sleep indicators, bone and muscle countermeasure adherence, mood check-ins, radiation logs, and cabin conditions into a unified dashboard. An illustrative health score, personal-baseline comparisons, and plain-language alerts help astronauts review changes and identify next steps. Guided relaxation, exercise tracking, manual entries, and astronaut-controlled sharing connect monitoring with practical action.

The prototype demonstrates local operation without continuous communication with Earth, using simulated and manually entered readings. Hardware connections and ground delivery are simulated.

StarX Health addresses the challenge of helping astronauts gather, evaluate, and act on health information during long-duration missions. By combining physical, mental, and environmental context, it aims to strengthen health awareness and support informed onboard decisions when ground support is limited. Clinical validation, stronger security, and real sensor integration are required before operational use.
details:
StarX Health, developed by Team StarX_TN, is an offline-first astronaut health-monitoring and self-management prototype. It brings health indicators, personal check-ins, and cabin conditions into one understandable interface, helping astronauts review changes and identify appropriate next steps during long-duration missions.

The project focuses on a simple principle: health monitoring should help the astronaut understand and act—not merely display numbers.

What Does It Do, and How Does It Work?

StarX Health follows a Collect → Understand → Act → Share by Choice workflow:

  1. Collect health information: The prototype accepts manual entries and validated JSON imports, alongside simulated sensor readings. Records use a common format containing the metric, value, unit, timestamp, and source.
  2. Present a clear health overview: An illustrative unified score is supported by separate views for heart, sleep, bone, muscle, mood, and radiation. Cabin CO₂, humidity, and temperature provide environmental context. Bone and muscle indicators are demonstration countermeasure-adherence proxies—not measurements of bone density or muscle mass.
  3. Highlight changes: Demo personal reference ranges and example historical trends show how readings differ from an astronaut’s usual patterns. Plain-language alerts explain the change and suggest what to review next.
  4. Support practical action: Astronauts can record mood, sleep, energy, and private journal notes; use guided relaxation timers; log exercise sessions; set in-app reminders; and maintain a radiation-dose history.
  5. Enable controlled collaboration: Astronauts select which categories to include in a health summary. Journal notes require separate permission. Summaries can be previewed, queued locally, or cancelled. Ground delivery is simulated in the current prototype.

The core interface operates locally. Offline caching and a self-contained HTML version demonstrate continued use without an active internet connection.

Benefits and Intended Impact

StarX Health aims to make health information easier to interpret when astronauts must take greater responsibility for recognizing changes themselves.

Its intended benefits include:

  • Greater onboard autonomy: Reviewing information and recording changes without waiting for an Earth link.
  • Less fragmented information: Bringing physical, mental, radiation, and environmental context into one workflow.
  • Clearer next steps: Connecting status information with check-ins, relaxation, exercise tracking, and further review.
  • More deliberate sharing: Allowing astronauts to control the information prepared for ground medical teams.
  • Continuity without hardware: Keeping the interface useful through manual entries and imports.

These are intended design benefits; improvements in health outcomes, workload, or mission safety have not yet been measured.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Application development: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, React, React DOM, and Vite.
  • Development environment: Node.js and npm.
  • Local data handling: JSON records, browser local storage, and service-worker caching.
  • Testing: Playwright with Chromium for functional, responsive-layout, persistence, consent, and offline checks.
  • Visual design: Lucide icons, the Manrope font, and screenshots from the working prototype.
  • Documentation and presentation: Python, python-pptx, Pillow, and CairoSVG, with LibreOffice and Poppler used for presentation review.
  • AI assistance: Arena.ai supported coding, written content, and generation of the orbital Earth artwork.

No physical sensor hardware was used to build or validate the current demonstration. Smartwatch, ECG patch, pulse oximeter, dosimeter, and cabin-sensor connections are simulated. Real Bluetooth, USB, and API adapters remain future work.

How Is the Project Creative?

The creativity lies in combining several needs into an astronaut-centered evaluation-and-action experience. Rather than treating heart readings, mood, exercise, radiation, and cabin conditions as unrelated information, StarX Health presents them together.

Its distinctive design choices include personal-baseline review, manual fallback, offline operation, plain-language guidance, and granular sharing permissions. The project builds on established monitoring ideas without claiming that every individual feature is new.

What Factors Did the Team Consider?

The design considered:

  • Communication limitations: Core activities should remain available without continuous ground contact.
  • Individual differences: An astronaut’s own reference patterns can provide more relevant context than a generic average.
  • Usability and workload: Short check-ins, readable status views, and responsive layouts should make routine interaction straightforward.
  • Consent and privacy: Sharing should be deliberate, with sensitive journal notes excluded by default.
  • Missing or inconsistent inputs: Manual fallback and import validation help maintain a usable workflow.
  • Medical responsibility: A demonstration score must not be treated as a diagnosis, exercise clearance, or radiation-safety decision.

Current Status and Next Steps

A working prototype with eight navigable sections has been completed, and 18 automated functional checks passed, including genuine offline reloads and sharing-permission tests.

The prototype uses simulated and manually entered data. Real sensor integration, live space-weather information, encrypted medical storage, authenticated ground delivery, clinician-reviewed rules, and operational validation are required before real-world deployment.
